mcqs.question: A styled `<div onclick="submit()">` is used in place of a `<button>` inside a form. What breaks as a result?
options: Nothing, as long as the click handler correctly calls the submit function
Only the visual styling differs; all interactive behavior stays identical
It becomes keyboard-unreachable and invisible to assistive tech unless tabindex, a keydown handler, and an ARIA role are all added manually, and it still won't trigger native form submission
The form submits twice due to a duplicate event firing
mcqs.explanation: A button element carries keyboard focusability, Enter/Space activation, an implicit accessible role, and native form-submission participation for free — none of that exists on a div by default, so all of it has to be manually reimplemented and the div still can't natively submit a form. Nothing here causes a double-submit, and the gap is far more than visual.

mcqs.question: An input has `type="email" required` and nothing else. What happens if a user leaves it empty and clicks submit, with no JavaScript on the page at all?
options: The form submits anyway since required only applies when JavaScript validation is present
The browser blocks submission, focuses the field, and shows a native validation message — no JavaScript required
The page silently reloads with no indication of the error
Nothing happens until the developer adds a submit event listener
mcqs.explanation: Native HTML validation runs entirely in the browser before any JavaScript executes — required blocks an empty submission and the browser handles focusing the field and showing feedback on its own. required doesn't depend on script being present at all; that's the entire point of native validation.

mcqs.question: A field uses `setCustomValidity('Passwords must match')` to flag a mismatch, and the developer later fixes the values so they match — but the field stays stuck as invalid. What's the likely bug?
options: setCustomValidity only works once per page load
The code never calls setCustomValidity('') to clear the error once the condition becomes valid again
Custom validity messages require a page reload to reset
The Constraint Validation API doesn't support clearing custom errors at all
mcqs.explanation: The browser has no way of knowing a custom validity error has been resolved unless the code explicitly calls setCustomValidity('') to clear it — forgetting that step is the single most common bug with this API. It can be called any number of times per page, doesn't require a reload, and clearing is a supported, expected part of the API.

mcqs.question: An input has a visible red error message next to it, but a screen reader user reports they have no idea an error exists. What's missing?
options: aria-describedby linking the input to the error text, so assistive tech associates the two
A larger font-size on the error message
Changing the error text's color to a brighter red
Adding a title attribute to the input
mcqs.explanation: Visual proximity between an input and an error message conveys nothing to a screen reader on its own — aria-describedby is what explicitly programmatically links the two, so the error gets announced with the field. Font size, color, and title attributes are all visual or low-value fixes that don't address the missing programmatic association.

mcqs.question: A numeric field has client-side `min="1" max="100"` and no equivalent check on the server. What's the actual risk?
options: None — client-side min/max is enforced by the browser for every request that reaches the server
A slightly worse error message if the value is invalid
A slower page load due to redundant validation
A crafted request sent directly to the server, bypassing the browser entirely, can submit any value outside 1–100 since nothing there enforces the bound
mcqs.explanation: Client-side constraints exist only inside the browser's form UI — a request built and sent directly (via a script, curl, or a modified devtools request) never passes through that check at all, so an unguarded server accepts whatever value arrives. This isn't about error message quality or performance; it's a real correctness and security gap if the server doesn't independently validate.

mcqs.question: A login form's password field has `autocomplete="off"`, added by a developer who assumed it improves security. What's the actual effect?
options: It has no measurable effect on security or usability in modern browsers
It forces the browser to encrypt the stored value before autofilling it
It degrades usability and can discourage password managers from generating and storing a strong unique password for the site
It prevents the field from being targeted by autofill-based phishing entirely, which is its intended purpose
mcqs.explanation: Modern browsers and password managers largely ignore or work around autocomplete="off" on password fields, but the attempt still degrades the autofill and password-generation experience for users, working against the intended security goal rather than achieving it. It doesn't add encryption and doesn't meaningfully block phishing-style attacks, which operate independent of this attribute.
